processing: The same cut needles as red rooibos, but the heap oxidation is skipped: the cut plant is dried quickly, by a more demanding method similar to green tea production, so it stays green instead of turning red.
harvest_season: Late summer harvest, January to April, cut at the same time as red rooibos; the difference is entirely in processing.
appearance_dry: Pale khaki-green needles and stems with a few yellowish pieces, lighter and more fragile-looking than the red version.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green to light gold, clear.
appearance_wet: Soft olive-green needles smelling of fresh hay and dried grass.
taste_profile: Light, grassy and hay-like with a honeyed sweetness and a mild green-tea-like freshness; thinner body than red rooibos and no bitterness.

brewing.notes: Slightly cooler water than red rooibos (85–95 °C) and 4–6 minutes keeps the fresh notes; boiling water and long steeps flatten it into something dull and papery. Excellent cold-brewed.

vintage_note: A newer product than red rooibos, made in small volumes and sold year-round without a harvest year on the pack. It loses its fresh, grassy character faster than the red version, so look for a best-before date at least 18 months away and use it within about a year of opening. Sold mostly as long-cut loose leaf and in a few tea-bag ranges; 'green rooibos' is sometimes used loosely on flavoured blends, so check the ingredient list.
description:
Green rooibos is rooibos that never went red. The same needle-leaved shrub from the Cederberg is cut at the same time of year, but instead of being bruised and heaped to oxidise, it is dried straight away, so it keeps its green colour and a much lighter, fresher taste.

The quick drying is the whole story. Red rooibos gets its honey, wood and vanilla from the hours in the oxidising heap; without that step the plant tastes of hay, sweet grass and a faint green-tea freshness. It also keeps more of the compounds that the oxidation would have changed, which is why it is marketed as the 'healthier' rooibos; treat that as marketing and judge it on taste.

Brew it a little more gently than red rooibos: water around 90 °C and four to six minutes gives a pale gold cup that is sweet and clean. Boiling water for ten minutes does not make it bitter, just flat. It is one of the best bases for a cold brew, since it has no astringency and the hay note turns into something like fresh melon when cold.

It is a small part of the rooibos crop and prices are a bit higher. Choose a long cut with visible green needles rather than a dusty short cut, and buy from a seller with turnover, because old green rooibos smells of nothing much.

If you want a caffeine-free green-tea stand-in for the evening, this is a better bet than most 'decaf green'. For more body, go back to classic red rooibos; for more sweetness, try honeybush.
history: Green rooibos is a variation on South African rooibos: the same plant, Aspalathus linearis, without the oxidation that gives ordinary rooibos its reddish-brown colour. Little is documented about who first made it or exactly when. Production resembles that of green tea and is more demanding than the red method, which is why it costs more, and the result is malty and slightly grassy, somewhat different from the red.
